responses_by_run.answer: Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show respect to the goddess, Arachne scornfully rejected the counsel and challenged Athena herself to a weaving contest [1]. After Arachne lost the competition, Athena destroyed her work in anger at the mortal's presumption [2]. When Arachne attempted to hang herself in despair, Athena saved her life but pronounced a terrible doom: she would dangle on a cord forever as a spider, and her punishment would extend to all her descendants, serving as an eternal example of the consequences of challenging the gods [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions. First, he stole fire and gave it to humans [1]. According to Apollodorus, when Zeus learned that Prometheus had hidden fire in a fennel stalk and given it to humans, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to nail Prometheus to Mount Caucasus, where an eagle devoured his liver daily as punishment [1]. Second, according to Hesiod, Prometheus attempted to deceive Zeus during a dispute over sacrificial portions at Mecone by dividing them unfairly, presenting Zeus with bones covered in fat while hiding the better meat [2]. Hesiod notes that Prometheus could not escape Zeus's heavy anger despite his cunning, and was bound with inextricable bonds and tormented by an eagle until Heracles freed him [3].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus cried out for help from other Cyclopes, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and departed [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and had his men cling to the middle sheep while he himself clung to the belly of the largest ram [1][2]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them, and Odysseus and his comrades escaped to their ship [1][2].

At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods celebrated the marriage with feast and song on Mount Pelion [1]. The marriage took place after Peleus seized Thetis despite her shape-shifting resistance, holding her fast as she transformed into fire, water, and various beasts until she resumed her original form [1]. Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear as a wedding gift, and Poseidon gave him immortal horses named Balius and Xanthus [1].

Demeter stopped the crops from growing because she was grieving over the loss of her daughter. She was 'wasting with yearning for her deep-bosomed daughter' [1] and vowed that she would never let fruit spring out of the ground until she beheld her own fair-faced daughter with her eyes [2]. Her daughter had been carried off by Pluto (with Zeus's help), and Demeter's yearning and wrath over this abduction caused her to withhold the growth of crops from the earth [3].

responses_by_run.answer: Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because the commander took his prize, Briseis. According to Homer's account, Achilles was angered that Agamemnon threatened to seize Briseis—the reward he had earned through his efforts in battle—while Agamemnon's own prize remained far greater [1]. Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain dishonored and toil to increase Agamemnon's wealth [1]. Apollodorus provides a more concise explanation, stating simply that Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of the priest Chryses [2].

Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show humility and ask the goddess for pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected her and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After the competition, Athena found Arachne's work flawless but was enraged by the girl's skill and defiance [2]. Athena destroyed Arachne's web and struck her repeatedly [2]. Arachne then attempted to hang herself, but Athena saved her from death while pronouncing a different doom: 'your fate shall be to dangle on a cord, and your posterity forever shall take your example, that your punishment may last forever!' [2]. Athena then sprinkled Arachne with magical herbs, causing her body to shrink and transform into a spider, condemning her to weave webs eternally as a permanent punishment for her presumption [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions: stealing fire from the gods and hiding it in a stalk of fennel to give to humans [1], and for attempting to deceive Zeus by dividing sacrificial portions unfairly at Mecone [2]. As punishment, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to bind Prometheus to Mount Caucasus with inextricable bonds and chains, driving a shaft through his middle [1]. An eagle was set upon him to devour his liver daily, which would grow back each night, prolonging his torment for many years until Heracles eventually freed him [1].
